summary: The March 2026 update gave Australia's longest-serving plug-in hybrid a 22.7kWh battery, 221kW and a locally developed suspension and steering tune, and reviewers agree the ride and steering are genuinely better than the pre-update car even if 20-inch wheels still let sharp bumps through. Where they split is value: the extra 86km of WLTP electric range and the unique seven-seat Aspire earn praise, but prices rose $1700-$3000 and the range now sits well above cheaper Chinese plug-in rivals that offer more EV range for less. The charging hardware is the consistent complaint, with a CHAdeMO DC port on a standard that is disappearing from Australian chargers and only 3.6kW AC charging.
pros: 86km of WLTP electric range from the new 22.7kWh pack, up from 20kWh and 84km NEDC on the pre-update car; CarsGuide saw about 80km in real-world urban running, enough to cover a typical Melbourne commute without starting the engine
The Aspire is the only seven-seat plug-in hybrid at this price - the BYD Sealion 6, Mazda CX-60 PHEV and Toyota RAV4 PHEV are all five-seat only
1600kg braked towing across the whole PHEV range, roughly double the BYD Sealion 6 Essential's 750kg and enough for a small camper or box trailer

Mitsubishi advertises a 10-year/200,000km warranty and 10 years of capped-price servicing (about $550 a year), but that term is conditional on every scheduled service being done inside the Mitsubishi dealer network; walk away from the dealer and the cover reverts to 5 years/100,000km. The drive battery is separately warranted for 8 years/160,000km

Springs, dampers and steering were re-tuned in South Australia for the 2026 update, and Australian reviewers report noticeably less float and better-weighted steering at speed than the car it replaces
cons: DC fast charging uses a CHAdeMO plug, a standard being decommissioned across Australian public charging networks, and AC charging is capped at 3.6kW so a full recharge takes about 6.5 hours on a home wallbox

The 1.2L/100km NEDC label figure only holds if you start every trip fully charged - Mitsubishi's own battery-depleted figure is 6.7L/100km, and CarsGuide measured around 10L/100km when the engine is actively charging the pack, so the running-cost case collapses for a buyer without home charging

The 2026 update added $1700-$3000 across the range, putting the ES at $58,990 and the Exceed Tourer at $74,490; reviewers call the flagship overpriced next to cheaper plug-in rivals with more electric range

The Aspire's third row leaves only 191 litres of boot behind it and is not covered by the curtain airbags, which extend to the first two rows only - it is a children-only occasional space, not a genuine seven-seater
The 2.4-litre engine is audibly coarse when it cuts in, described by reviewers as sounding like a vacuum cleaner from inside the cabin
